doc_summary: Bowman argues for a 'bumpers' alignment strategy: rather than needing to solve alignment outright, build and test many largely independent safeguards (audits, red-teaming, post-deployment monitoring) so misalignment can be caught and corrected via iterative rewind-and-retry. The post is a high-level strategy sketch and says little directly about eval realism.

items.claim: Prefers building and testing many largely independent lines of defense for catching misalignment over relying on a single method or on solving alignment outright, because no one check is trusted to be sufficient.
items.quote: we'd aim to build up many largely-independent lines of defense that allow us to catch and respond to early signs of misalignment.

items.claim: Prefers running alignment audits with many methods in parallel (interpretability, prompting outside the human/assistant frame, behavioral red-teaming) over any single behavioral probe, because convincing evidence comes from converging independent methods.
items.quote: we perform [alignment audits](https://www.anthropic.com/research/auditing-hidden-objectives) on the system under construction, using many methods in parallel. We’d draw on mechanistic interpretability, prompting outside the human/assistant frame, etc.

items.claim: Treats implementing and testing safeguards that enable course-correction after building or deploying a misaligned model as a top priority, which makes detection of behaviors like reward-tampering and alignment-faking the central testing target.
items.quote: treat it as a top priority to implement and test safeguards that allow us to course-correct if we turn out to have built or deployed a misaligned model

items.claim: Chooses which behaviors to test by focusing on specific known warning signs, such as generalized reward-tampering and alignment-faking, rather than generic misbehavior.
items.quote: If we see signs of misalignment—perhaps warning signs for [generalized reward-tampering](https://www.anthropic.com/research/reward-tampering) or [alignment-faking](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-faking)—we attempt to quickly, approximately identify the cause.

items.claim: Treats 'no observed warning signs' as only provisional evidence of alignment ('appears, as best we can tell'), and keeps monitoring after deployment, since a clean audit result is not trusted as final.
items.quote: We then begin rolling out the system in earnest, both for internal R&D and external use, but keep substantial monitoring measures in place that provide additional opportunities to catch misalignment.

items.claim: Pursues iterative rewind-and-retry when audits find misalignment, but abandons the alignment attempt and documents why if failures repeat consistently.
items.quote: Or, we are *repeatedly* failing in consistent ways, change plans and try to articulate as best we can why alignment doesn’t seem tractable.

items.claim: Frames claims as a hypothesis to be tested, with explicit uncertainty about convergence and about whether a converged model is truly aligned, rather than asserting safety outright.
items.quote: We are not certain of this hypothesis, but we think it’s important to consider.

items.claim: Distrusts the assumption that a single-shot alignment attempt will succeed (like a beginner's bowling throw), and so relies on catching failures instead of assuming alignment.
items.quote: If a child is bowling for the first time, and they just aim at the pins and throw, they’re almost certain to miss.

items.claim: Plans to scale up interpretability audits, behavioral red-teaming, and post-deployment monitoring, and is hiring to build out this work.
items.quote: This would involve significantly improving and scaling up our use of tools like mechanistic interpretability audits, behavioral red-teaming, and early post-deployment monitoring.
